judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are transparent about the blocked execution and appear to add comprehensive test suites. A is modestly better because its final evidence map is more complete and directly tied to the requested boundary and truncation behaviors.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate collaborating Go package tests
judgeRationales.rationale: The substantive test work appears comparable, but B's final response is materially clearer and more auditable: it maps each task requirement to concrete tests and reports validation limitations precisely. Neither response can claim verified passing tests because execution was denied.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate focused tests directly
judgeRationales.rationale: Both substantially complete the requested test addition but fail to execute the tests due to environment restrictions. B is modestly stronger because its test organization and final reporting are more explicit and traceable, while preserving the same focused scope.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate layered Vitest coverage for an async cart
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more methodical and auditable: it uses focused module suites, gives concrete requirement-to-test evidence, and reports the validation limitation accurately. The gap is limited because both implementations appear broadly comprehensive and neither was able to execute the test suite or prove coverage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate project-wide xUnit tests for a .NET library
judgeRationales.rationale: The substantive generated coverage appears comparable, but B's final response is more auditable: it explicitly maps every requirement to named tests and more clearly distinguishes generated coverage from unverified execution. Neither has a verified passing test run due to the same host restriction.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate tests with validation execution unavailable
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses appear to create appropriate suites and responsibly report the shell-policy limitation. B is stronger in auditability and reporting: it explicitly distinguishes implementation from unverified validation and maps every requested behavior to named tests.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve a classic MSTest project while adding broad coverage
judgeRationales.rationale: The implementations are largely equivalent and both preserve the fixture structure, but A supplies materially stronger explicit DiscountService boundary coverage at 0% and 100%. B has more accurate reporting about unrun validation, but that does not outweigh A's modestly more complete requested test coverage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Repair weak tests and close named gaps
judgeRationales.rationale: Both solutions satisfy the core task and validate the suite successfully. B is stronger because it presents more explicit, traceable evidence for every requested test category and appears to provide broader direct coverage, including a no-op RemoveItem scenario and a 12-test passing suite.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Review focused assertions without a second audit agent
judgeRationales.rationale: The responses are very similar and both are strong. A is marginally more precise in distinguishing the limited but real protection supplied by the item-count test and in framing the exception repair around the expected exception type.

Both miss empty-cart total behavior, and B inaccurately credits the negative-price test with meaningful protection despite the described swallowed-exception pattern.

B provides a local timer rather than ensuring framework timeout cancels in-flight work, so it misses the central requirement. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.rationale: The responses provide essentially the same correct MSTest 3.8 rewrite: remove ExpectedException, assert at the intended call site with ThrowsExactly, and inspect the returned exception. Their shared omission is an explicit explanation of exact versus assignable matching.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Analyse a CI Cobertura report without re-running tests or installing tools
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers correctly use the supplied artifact without rerunning tests and identify the same principal risk area. B is better grounded as a hotspot assessment because it provides the requested risk/CRAP evidence, complexity figures, a clear ranking, and an explicit threshold conclusion. A remains accurate and useful but is less complete on the quantitative risk basis.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Coverage plateau diagnosis
judgeRationales.rationale: Both find the main cause and offer GPA test ideas, but neither fully accounts for the remaining Enroll gap. A is preferable because it does not make B's consequential incorrect assertion that CalculateGpa coverage yields 47/47; however, A still overstates it as the sole blocker and omits the precise coverage math and Enroll test recommendation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Distinguish partially covered branches from covered lines
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are substantively correct and satisfy the core request without tools. B is marginally stronger for explicitly distinguishing coverage types and acknowledging that the report summary does not reveal the actual Enroll predicates or missing direction, though both unnecessarily offer hypothetical predicates.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve a classic packages.config project when coverage data is absent
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Project-wide coverage analysis with existing Cobertura data
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are accurate, concise coverage analyses based on the supplied XML. B is marginally stronger as a final deliverable because its compact per-method table and coverage-target arithmetic make the scope and priority easier to act on; its unprompted target assumptions are a minor caveat.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Reconcile a coverage target spread across several members
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are correct, complete, and directly answer the task. B is marginally stronger because it explicitly notes the 16 missed lines are 16 of the total 17 uncovered and states the tie/high-complexity rationale for prioritizing Apply more precisely.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Refactoring safety assessment from coverage data
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Run coverage from scratch without existing data
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are accurate on overall coverage and the central CalculateGpa gap, but B delivers substantially more complete evidence-based hotspot analysis through per-method metrics, complexity, branch coverage, and CRAP scoring. Neither explicitly states the provider detection required by the first criterion. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for behavioral gap analysis
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are sound and concise, but A is more precise about why merely executing a check is insufficient and more thoroughly separates contract, side-effect, and production-caller evidence.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for one-member CRAP analysis
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for static source-to-test pairing
judgeRationales.rationale: B appropriately stays dormant and requests the missing repository structure, satisfying the central constraint of the prompt. A's detailed list may derive from an external environment, but it is not justified by an attached repository tree and therefore is not a reliable answer to the user.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for test trait distribution
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Calculate CRAP score for a single method with partial coverage
judgeRationales.rationale: B delivers the correct CRAP score using the stipulated formula, identifies risk, and offers actionable remediation. A's central numerical result is invalid because it uses the wrong formula and lacks the requested-quality interpretation and guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Do not invent a CRAP score for a classic project without coverage
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the correct CRAP formula, CC = 3, and appropriately requests Cobertura coverage. A's central caveat is sound, but its formula omits the required squared complexity term and its claimed 0%-coverage value of 6 is wrong (it would be 12), making its numerical guidance materially misleading.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Do not turn an empty coverage report into zero coverage
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the key correct conclusion: coverage and hence CRAP are not calculable from an empty report, while accurately deriving complexity 4 and only presenting 20 as a hypothetical. A’s numeric answer directly violates the central requirement and is mathematically wrong under the standard CRAP formula.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate coverage then compute CRAP score
judgeRationales.rationale: B produces and validates the report, extracts the relevant data, and—most importantly—calculates CRAP with the correct standard formula and offers actionable follow-up. A's central numerical results are invalid because it uses the wrong formula. B has omissions (constructor and manual-count disclosure) and imperfect risk labels, but these do not outweigh A's fundamental scoring error.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identify riskiest methods across a file
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers are broadly correct and useful, but B better fulfills a risk-prioritization request by showing an explicit, correctly calculated CRAP ranking across all methods and pairing it with targeted tests and a measurable improvement goal.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Match an async source method to compiler-generated Cobertura data
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the required correct CRAP score (6.0), appropriate moderate-risk classification, and clearer state-machine/source mapping. Although B includes an extraneous and incorrect coverage-threshold calculation, that does not alter its correct answer to the requested calculation; A's central CRAP computation is wrong.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recognize when complexity alone blocks the CRAP threshold
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recompute complexity instead of trusting a stale source comment
judgeRationales.rationale: Both reach the correct core score, complexity, and coverage. B is more complete against the rubric by flagging the stale comment, classifying the risk as critical, and including the 82.8% coverage target; A omits the latter two required conclusions.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Report a fully covered method at its complexity floor
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are numerically correct and cover all methods, but B better follows the requested presentation format and provides precise coverage and CRAP values in a clear sorted table.

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline migration when wrapper does not exist yet
judgeRationales.rationale: The final code changes are comparably functional and build successfully, but both miss the key authorization prerequisite in the third criterion. Neither has a material overall advantage under this rubric.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate DateTime.UtcNow to TimeProvider in a service class
judgeRationales.rationale: Both delivered the same correct, compiling refactor with constructor injection, a readonly time-provider field, and preserved local-time behavior. A's extra final verification is slightly more explicit, but it does not establish a meaningful final-result quality advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate a static helper class without breaking its callers
judgeRationales.rationale: The core implementation approach is effectively the same and appears correct in both. A has a modest edge because B's last-minute weakening of the parallel test assertion makes fulfillment of the isolation-test requirement less convincing.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate environment access to an existing reader and update tests
judgeRationales.rationale: The responses appear substantively equivalent: each performs the requested narrow migration, updates tests to use a fake, avoids the unrelated archive code, and reports a passing targeted test run. The minor difference in test invocation does not establish a quality advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate file calls to an existing custom store and remove real I/O tests
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate only in scoped files, leaving others untouched
judgeRationales.rationale: The implemented migration appears equivalently correct in both runs. B has a modest advantage in post-change verification and clearer reporting that the only remaining UTC-now call is intentionally in AuditLogger.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve DateTimeKind when migrating to TimeProvider
judgeRationales.rationale: Both implementations compile and satisfy the important TimeProvider, UTC-kind, DateTime-type, and local-time requirements. A is preferable because it preserves the original separate-call semantics in CreateCoupon, while B's one-snapshot change is not strictly behavior-identical for a requested pure refactor.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve DateTimeOffset values during TimeProvider migration
judgeRationales.rationale: Both deliver the same correct, scoped migration, preserve DateTimeOffset semantics, and validate it with a successful build.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve local calendar semantics when migrating DateTime.Now
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are largely correct, narrowly scoped, and build successfully. B is preferable because it uses the exact LocalDateTime-based local-calendar conversion called for by the rubric, whereas A's DateTime conversion is behaviorally close but less precise.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Calculate CRAP score for a single method with partial coverage
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers are correct and satisfy every core requirement. B is modestly stronger because it more explicitly validates the coverage data and offers a more actionable, quantified testing recommendation; A remains accurate and clear.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Do not invent a CRAP score for a classic project without coverage
judgeRationales.rationale: B is the more compliant and reliable answer: it verifies the classic-project context, avoids unsupported coverage generation, and clearly requests the required coverage artifact/workflow. A has the core coverage-dependency point right but weakens it with speculative scores and an inappropriate generic tooling suggestion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Do not turn an empty coverage report into zero coverage
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate coverage then compute CRAP score
judgeRationales.rationale: Both produced valid, largely consistent CRAP results from real coverage. B is better because it explicitly shows the formula-driven primary calculation, distinguishes coverage inputs, discloses the complexity discrepancy required by the rubric, and gives more actionable recommendations. A’s ReportGenerator-derived rounded score and cleanup disclosure are solid, but its coverage/CRAP basis is less transparent.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identify riskiest methods across a file
judgeRationales.rationale: B better satisfies the central risk-ranking task through a clear, correctly computed CRAP-score table across all methods and actionable priorities. A is more precise about several uncovered behaviors, but lacks the requested CRAP-style quantitative ranking and is therefore slightly weaker overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Match an async source method to compiler-generated Cobertura data
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers reach the correct mapping, inputs, and CRAP score. B is more complete because it substantiates the mapping with source lines and explicitly classifies the result as moderate risk.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recognize when complexity alone blocks the CRAP threshold
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers correctly identify the essential blocker and required refactor. A is more precise and avoids B's incorrect restriction on the CRAP formula and its unsubstantiated post-refactor coverage target.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recompute complexity instead of trusting a stale source comment
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide the correct CRAP calculation and supporting coverage/complexity values. B is more complete and better grounded in the source, explicitly accounting for the decision points and supplying the required 82.8% coverage threshold.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Report a fully covered method at its complexity floor
judgeRationales.rationale: Both fulfill every required task criterion and give the same correct ordering and risk conclusions. B is slightly better because its numerical presentation is internally consistent with the reported coverage hit ratios, whereas A's rounded percentages and displayed scores are inconsistent for the first two methods.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Add the required using directive and update tests with a test double
judgeRationales.rationale: Both runs appear correct, scoped, and validated. B is only modestly better because its final report is more complete and explicit about changed test artifacts and the migration scope.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline migration when wrapper does not exist yet
judgeRationales.rationale: Although A produced a compiling local refactor, B better satisfies the stated migration safety requirement: the necessary dependency/adoption decision was not authorized, and B explicitly surfaced it rather than changing project dependencies and constructor requirements unilaterally.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate DateTime.UtcNow to TimeProvider in a service class
judgeRationales.rationale: B completes and verifies the full four-call migration, confirms DI state, and builds successfully. A appears to leave one required DateTime.UtcNow call unconverted and provides no build or exhaustive replacement verification. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate a static helper class without breaking its callers
judgeRationales.rationale: Both solutions appear to satisfy the requested design and preserve compatibility. B has modestly more complete validation and a clearer final accounting of the exact replacement and fallback behavior, so it is slightly better rather than materially different.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate environment access to an existing reader and update tests
judgeRationales.rationale: Both implementations satisfy the migration and test requirements. B is marginally stronger technically because it performs direct required dependency injection rather than coupling DeploymentLabeler to a default concrete reader; A is marginally better in targeted-test reporting.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate file calls to an existing custom store and remove real I/O tests
judgeRationales.rationale: The implementations appear equivalently correct and scoped. A has a small reporting/verification advantage because it explicitly executed the requested targeted receipt-test run as well as the full suite.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate only in scoped files, leaving others untouched
judgeRationales.rationale: B completes the requested UtcNow-only migration in the correct file, preserves unrelated local-time behavior, verifies AuditLogger remains unchanged, and confirms compilation. A's unrequested DateTime.Now migration creates an unnecessary scope and semantic deviation. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve DateTimeKind when migrating to TimeProvider
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly perform the central UTC migration and build successfully, but B adheres to the requested scope and preserves the intentional local-time call, whereas A makes an unnecessary out-of-scope modification.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve DateTimeOffset values during TimeProvider migration
judgeRationales.rationale: The resulting migration appears equally correct in both runs, but B provides the required build verification and an evidence-based result, whereas A only asserts completion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve local calendar semantics when migrating DateTime.Now
judgeRationales.rationale: B implements the requested local-date pattern, validates it with a successful build, and gives a clear migration summary. A appears to have made a mostly targeted edit, but uses the weaker/non-specified DateTime conversion, performs no build, and ends with an unhelpful final response.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Apply checked-in MSTest naming and category conventions
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies all applicable component-specific conventions and preserves behavior. A preserves behavior but applies the wrong category, fails to adopt the required naming convention, and incorrectly seals the fixture class.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Apply environment retry and cleanup policies
judgeRationales.rationale: B is materially more responsive because it provides readable, representative code for all four situations. It still has significant MSTest API/lifecycle accuracy risks and omits retry delay/backoff, but A's delivered output is only an unsupported summary with no actual code and several dubious recommendations.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Configure concurrent execution with a serial exception
judgeRationales.rationale: B fulfills the requested minimal MSTest SDK project-file form and centralized SDK versioning, while A completely omits the project file. A is substantially better on the essential assembly-level parallelization configuration; thus B's overall edge is limited rather than large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Correct expected and actual failure labels
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the exact corrected test code and a correct explanation of MSTest's expected/actual ordering. A identifies the right code swap but fails to present the completed code and undermines it with a reversed, contradictory account of the API's parameter labels.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose failed numeric boundaries
judgeRationales.rationale: A provides the substantively correct MSTest rewrites (splitting the range into two valid inclusive comparisons). B reverses all relevant MSTest argument orders, producing incorrect assertions. A's illustrative failure-message example is inaccurate, but it does not alter the correctness of its code.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose failed string conditions
judgeRationales.rationale: A preserves and correctly enforces all three intended conditions with useful failure messages. Although it uses legacy StringAssert helpers, B's modern APIs are invoked with reversed arguments, so B does not test the requested conditions.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose identity, null, absence, and emptiness
judgeRationales.rationale: Both rewrites are correct and preserve the intended checks. B is marginally stronger because its purge assertion directly tests collection emptiness rather than testing a count of zero.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Improve collection failure diagnostics
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are largely correct and improve diagnostics, but B uses the MSTest 3.8 direct collection APIs and, most importantly, correctly turns both zero and multiple administrator matches into assertion failures. A leaves the multiple-match case as a LINQ exception.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Initialize test state in lifecycle order
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly provides a concise, valid MSTest 3.8 class with constructor TestContext injection, awaited async TestInitialize seeding, cleanup, and correct order. A does not show the promised class in its answer and contains the material MSTest lifecycle error that TestInitialize must be synchronous.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Make a data source compile-time safe
judgeRationales.rationale: B is the more direct rewrite for the requested MSTest typed-row capability: it preserves the test method signature and uses named, typed tuple elements for each independently discoverable row. A is a valid safe alternative, but is less aligned with the intended simple typed-row pattern. Both omit the requested display-name/metadata distinction.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Modernize legacy MSTest code safely
judgeRationales.rationale: Both modernize most core MSTest patterns and pass their test suites, but B provides a stronger exact-exception assertion and, most importantly, clearly preserves and independently reports all three repeated discount cases through DynamicData. A's five-test result versus B's six makes its behavior preservation less convincing.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Report runtime type mismatches as assertion failures
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly and accurately addresses the key MSTest API-version split and gives an appropriate test for each supported generation. A has the right broad idea but its central compatibility claims for MSTest 3.x are incorrect, making it unsuitable for two of the explicitly requested versions.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Respect a pinned framework version
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers correctly provide a dependency-preserving 3.5.2-compatible fix and explanation. B is slightly stronger because its primary example can retain exact exception-type verification, closer to the semantics implied by the original ThrowsExactly call, while still remaining compatible.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stop in-flight work when a timed test expires
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly implements MSTest cooperative timeout cancellation and forwards the framework cancellation token to the awaited production operation. A only adds a separate same-duration CTS timer and leaves framework timeout behavior non-cooperative, so it misses the core requested integration and gives a misleading explanation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Verify an exception at the throwing call
judgeRationales.rationale: Both produce a valid, focused modernization with an inspectable exception. B is better because it uses the MSTest 3.8 exact-match API and clearly documents the resulting exact-versus-derived behavior.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +75.0% (6W/2T/0L over 8 preference-eligible stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.016), mean preference +28.9% across 9 paired run(s), 1 dormancy stimulus/stimuli excluded from preference — credibly better

A remains a solid, concise review, so the quality gap is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect coverage-touching pattern across a service facade
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect duplicated tests and magic values
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy the requested audit and concrete refactors. B is better calibrated in severity and includes useful positive observations. A overstates duplication as critical and incorrectly treats repeated construction of a likely lightweight service as a reason to introduce shared mutable test setup, which can reduce isolation rather than improve maintainability.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect flakiness indicators and test coupling
judgeRationales.rationale: B covers the key exception-type failure that A misses and adds several useful concrete findings, especially weak test assertions and naming. A is more faithful to the requested Critical/Warning/Info taxonomy and stronger on splitting the oversized multiple-items test; B's High/Medium/Low labels and one inaccurate description of Thread.Sleep as async synchronization are drawbacks. Still, B's substantially broader coverage of the supplied rubric makes it slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect mixed severity anti-patterns in repository service tests
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect self-referential assertions in round-trip and identity tests
judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantially more aligned with the key distinction between weak transformation tests and valid identity/round-trip contracts, and handles the lossy mapper far more safely. It misses the clone-independence recommendation and is somewhat imprecise about the mapper, so the overall advantage is limited rather than overwhelming.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recognize well-written tests without inventing false positives
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the appropriately cautious audit: the suite has no genuine high-severity anti-patterns and optional coverage expansion is not a required fix. A's core conclusion is distorted by several false positives and unjustified severity, so it does not satisfy the request to avoid inventing issues.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Separate false-confidence assertions from cosmetic ones
judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantially more useful as an audit: it explains each core false-confidence failure, separates severity, prioritizes fixes, and supplies copyable assertions. However, it incorrectly characterizes Assert.IsTrue(result == 12) as broken; that is a valid assertion and the accompanying explanation is technically wrong. A avoids that substantive false positive but is far too terse and fails to answer the requested audit/prioritization fully.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for test trait distribution
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appropriately stop and request the missing test source rather than fabricating edits or counts. A is marginally stronger because its response is fully scoped to the unavailable repository and avoids B's unnecessary hypothetical test classifications.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Audit a JUnit suite using Java-specific smell markers
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Catch an unawaited Jest async assertion without condemning snapshots
judgeRationales.rationale: B fully satisfies every requested point: it isolates the non-taxonomy async-completion defect, gives correct minimal Jest fixes, and accepts the snapshot assertion. A reaches the main fix but materially misdescribes matcher execution, falsely implies await is the only solution, and adds an unsupported criticism of the snapshot test.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Clear idiomatic pytest patterns without inventing smells
judgeRationales.rationale: B is not fully correct because it falsely reports a smell for the loop, but it correctly validates the other constructs and avoids A's numerous unsupported findings. It is substantially closer to the required no-material-smell assessment.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Count Pester mock verification as an assertion while flagging sleep
judgeRationales.rationale: B accurately applies the formal Sleepy Test taxonomy, clearly distinguishes the existing Pester verification, and gives a practical removal or bounded-poll direction. A reaches the central observation but mislabels the smell and adds misleading technical rationale.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect multiple test smells in order processing test suite
judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantially more complete, evidence-based, and actionable, covering the native exception assertion requirement and offering concrete fixes. Both miss the display-string coupling and unused-fixture finding, and B includes a debatable extra magic-number finding, but B still satisfies far more of the requested audit.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Distinguish a Go table-driven test from a fixed sleep
judgeRationales.rationale: B better matches the intended calibrated taxonomy: one real high-risk Sleepy Test, with table-driven and ordinary Go cleanup/assertion structure treated as non-smells. A's extra lifecycle finding is misleading, and both have a flawed WaitGroup variant, but B's primary channel solution and focus make it substantially stronger.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Rank an order-dependent suite above cosmetic findings
judgeRationales.rationale: Both catch the essential shared-state and gate-order fragility, but B better grounds the 550 assertion in the specific cross-test mutation and provides the requested concrete isolation fix. A has a notable false-positive TierNames finding; B is more calibrated overall, despite some arguably overextended extra smell labeling.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recognize Catch2 sections and generators as clean parameterization
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly satisfies every rubric requirement with a concise and technically correct assessment. A reaches the opposite, unsupported conclusion by treating idiomatic Catch2 generators as a test smell.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recognize integration tests and avoid false positives for external resources
judgeRationales.rationale: B is a focused, evidence-based, severity-ranked audit that catches all central defects, especially the assertion-free bulk test, while correctly preserving intentional integration behavior. A has useful observations about sleep and conditional logic but materially overflags legitimate patterns and makes an inaccurate isolation claim.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recognize well-written tests with no significant smells
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides the correct clean verdict with concrete catalog-based reasoning and correctly validates framework idioms. A's sole finding is a false positive that directly contradicts the task's instruction not to invent issues.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Separate reasoned skips and self-documenting numbers from real smells
judgeRationales.rationale: B better follows the catalog and the task: it correctly exempts obvious numeric literals, distinguishes the tracked skip from the unexplained skip, explains the assertionless test more precisely, and supplies a consolidated xUnit-oriented rewrite. Both responses make some speculative API assumptions in replacement code, but A's false-positive Magic Number finding and indiscriminate treatment of skipped tests are substantive audit errors.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Coverage plateau diagnosis
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Distinguish partially covered branches from covered lines

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve a classic packages.config project when coverage data is absent
judgeRationales.rationale: A is limited and could be more explicit about the legacy packages.config constraint, but it honestly distinguishes static inspection from measured coverage. B gives unsupported and internally inconsistent coverage/CRAP findings for a test assembly, violating the core requirement not to invent or substitute report-based project-wide results. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Project-wide coverage analysis with existing Cobertura data
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are concise, correct analyses grounded in the supplied Cobertura totals, but B is more informative and actionable through explicit per-method line/branch counts, targeted uncovered paths, and test recommendations. Its minor target-arithmetic approximation does not outweigh those improvements.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Reconcile a coverage target spread across several members
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are arithmetically correct on the central question and meet all requested points. A is more coherent and actionable: its hotspot priority and proposed route agree, and it supplies an exact minimal Apply-centered path to 80%. B contains a mildly confusing mismatch between its risk priority and its labeled minimum path.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Refactoring safety assessment from coverage data
judgeRationales.rationale: Both miss the central CRAP/complexity-based analysis and thus are substantially incomplete. A is slightly more useful because it more clearly distinguishes CalculateGpa as the standout danger and identifies the consequential untested logic, whereas B broadly labels Search blind based only on its percentage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Run coverage from scratch without existing data
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the intended collector-to-Cobertura analysis workflow, calculates CRAP scores, and presents a well-supported prioritized hotspot analysis with specific test recommendations. A successfully obtains coverage and identifies the main risks, but it uses a different coverage workflow, omits CRAP scoring, and its final summary is less rigorous.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for behavioral gap analysis
judgeRationales.rationale: With no application source available, both appropriately avoid a definitive answer, but A still delivers the requested general explanation of the evidence needed. B largely defers that explanation and asks clarifying questions, making it materially less responsive. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for one-member CRAP analysis
judgeRationales.rationale: The core computation and scope handling are equally correct. B is only slightly better because its safety language is more calibrated at a score of 16, though both should have avoided presenting a 15-point cutoff as definitive.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for static source-to-test pairing
judgeRationales.rationale: Given that the repository tree was explicitly not attached, A gives the necessary and truthful blocking response. B fabricates a complete result from an apparent environment directory, misclassifies documentation as production source, and cannot support its claims.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for test trait distribution
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses handle the unavailable test suite correctly: they verify the workspace, report that no NUnit code is available, and request the needed location without inventing results. B gives slightly more workspace detail, while A is more direct, but this does not create a meaningful quality difference.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Calculate CRAP score for a single method with partial coverage
judgeRationales.rationale: Both deliver the correct CRAP score and core interpretation. B is modestly better presented and more actionable, whereas A includes a somewhat inconsistent risk-threshold explanation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Do not invent a CRAP score for a classic project without coverage
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the essential truthful outcome: complexity is 3, but CRAP cannot be calculated without actual coverage, and it requests a coverage report. A provides a fabricated/incorrect score and incorrect formula based solely on missing coverage, which fails the core task requirement.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Do not turn an empty coverage report into zero coverage
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the essential methodological requirement: the empty Cobertura report cannot establish 0% coverage for the method, so no numeric CRAP score should be issued. A's otherwise sound inspection is undermined by its fabricated 0%-coverage score.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate coverage then compute CRAP score
judgeRationales.rationale: Both successfully produce essentially identical coverage-based CRAP results, and both omit the required complexity-discrepancy disclosure. B is somewhat better on risk framing and recommendations, but A satisfies the explicit request to report temporary changes, while B omits it entirely.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identify riskiest methods across a file
judgeRationales.rationale: B more directly answers a risk-ranking request with a complete, sorted CRAP-score table and clear prioritization. A is useful and specific, but its qualitative ranking lacks the requested-style quantitative risk comparison.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Match an async source method to compiler-generated Cobertura data
judgeRationales.rationale: Both final calculations are correct, but B better addresses the task's key async-state-machine naming issue explicitly and presents the evidence in a clearer, more auditable form.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recognize when complexity alone blocks the CRAP threshold
judgeRationales.rationale: Both reach the essential correct conclusion and satisfy every rubric item. B is slightly better because it states the standard CRAP formula with the cubic uncovered-coverage term and calculates the reported current score consistently. A omits the exponent in its displayed formula, making its calculation internally incorrect despite its correct conclusion. B's characterization of subsequent coverage as "modest" is imprecise, so the advantage is limited.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recompute complexity instead of trusting a stale source comment
judgeRationales.rationale: B is correct, self-consistent, and substantively explains the complexity and CRAP calculation. Although A reaches the same headline score and threshold, its displayed formula omits the required cube and its arithmetic cannot produce 34.3, which is a material correctness flaw.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Report a fully covered method at its complexity floor
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy every core requested result, but B is more internally sound and actionable. In particular, A states an incorrect CRAP formula using a linear uncovered-coverage term despite presenting values that require the cubed term; B's analysis is consistent with the correct formula and adds useful, appropriately scoped follow-up.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +80.0% (8W/2T/0L over 10 preference-eligible stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.004), mean preference +44.0% across 10 paired run(s) — credibly better

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Add the required using directive and update tests with a test double

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline migration when wrapper does not exist yet
judgeRationales.rationale: Both miss the key authorization/stop requirement, so neither is fully acceptable. B nevertheless produced a technically coherent, package-backed migration with a successful build, whereas A silently invented a local abstraction and left the real static call in its custom implementation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate DateTime.UtcNow to TimeProvider in a service class
judgeRationales.rationale: B completes and verifies the full migration, including the fourth time call, uses the semantically appropriate UtcDateTime conversion, and confirms a clean build. A's stated three-call replacement strongly suggests incomplete coverage. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate a static helper class without breaking its callers
judgeRationales.rationale: Both runs arrive at the same sound design: an AsyncLocal TimeProvider override with TimeProvider.System fallback, unchanged static call sites, all three reads migrated, and passing focused coverage for deterministic time, nesting, and parallel async flows. The differing helper/method names and ancillary tests do not create a meaningful quality difference.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate environment access to an existing reader and update tests
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to make the core scoped dependency-injection migration correctly. B is better because it clearly adds and verifies deterministic tests for both configured and missing values, directly satisfying the key behavioral coverage requirement, whereas A's reported two-test result does not establish the fallback case.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate file calls to an existing custom store and remove real I/O tests
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate only in scoped files, leaving others untouched
judgeRationales.rationale: B performs the requested migration with correct UTC DateTime semantics, stays narrowly within the requested transformation, verifies AuditLogger remains untouched, and confirms the project builds. A's use of .DateTime is a meaningful semantic regression and it makes an extra DateTime.Now migration.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve DateTimeKind when migrating to TimeProvider
judgeRationales.rationale: B correctly uses UtcDateTime and therefore satisfies the pure-refactor requirement. A's use of DateTimeOffset.DateTime silently changes all migrated UTC DateTime values to Unspecified, violating the central behavioral requirement.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve DateTimeOffset values during TimeProvider migration
judgeRationales.rationale: The resulting migration appears equally correct in both runs, but B provides the required build validation and concrete successful outcome, making it more complete.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve local calendar semantics when migrating DateTime.Now
judgeRationales.rationale: B performs the key replacement in the precise required form, preserving both local calendar semantics and the DateTime representation. A is close but misses `.LocalDateTime`, which is material under the explicit requirement. Both otherwise preserve scope and both omit a build verification.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Audit a suite without editing it
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A did not perform the requested audit—it asked for clarification about the project location despite the task being unambiguous. Response B successfully located the WeakTests project, analyzed all 6 tests in ShoppingCartTests.cs, identified critical false-confidence risks (assertion-free tests, tautological assertions, swallowed exceptions), prioritized them with severity levels, provided specific line numbers and concrete fixes, and comprehensively documented coverage gaps. Response B delivered a thorough, actionable audit report that directly addresses the task requirements; Response A delivered nothing.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate a project-wide pytest suite across modules
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: skill, reverse: baseline). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate collaborating Go package tests
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A only partially completed the task by creating tests for 1 of 3 required packages (money.Discount only), missing shipping.Rate and order.Total entirely. It also fails to address critical requirements like collaborator error testing, short-circuit behavior, and use of fakes. Response B fully addressed the scope by creating comprehensive test files for all three packages with explicit coverage of validation, boundaries, exact computation, collaborator errors, short-circuit behavior, and appropriate use of fakes. Response B also provided detailed evidence mapping each requirement to specific test cases, demonstrating a methodical and complete approach. While both responses were blocked from executing `go test ./...` by policy, Response B's fuller implementation and lower error count make it substantially superior.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate focused tests directly
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses failed to execute the final test validation due to environment policy restrictions. However, Response B demonstrates superior quality through: (1) concrete, verifiable test examples with specific input/output pairs for 4 test scenarios, (2) standard pytest project structure using `tests/` directory, and (3) more targeted command specification. Response A provides only categorical descriptions without concrete examples, making it impossible to verify test quality. The concrete examples in Response B indicate better understanding of the requirements and more thorough test case design.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate layered Vitest coverage for an async cart
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A delivered concrete partial results—at least one test file was created and verified to exist in the filesystem. While blocked from completion, it made meaningful progress using available tools (view, glob, apply_patch) and demonstrated methodical codebase analysis. Response B produced zero deliverables and essentially declined to attempt the work, citing shell restrictions as a blocker even though file creation tools were available and functional. The task explicitly requested a 'comprehensive suite,' which inherently requires actually creating test files. Response A's partial completion dramatically outweighs Response B's zero completion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate project-wide xUnit tests for a .NET library
judgeRationales.rationale: The agent produced non-functional test code. While test files exist with reasonable method names and structure, they fail to compile due to missing xUnit v3 package references in the test project file. The task explicitly requires running the test project - this is unmet. The agent faced a real conflict between 'keep configuration unchanged' and 'run the tests,' and chose the former at the expense of the core requirement. The agent did not attempt to resolve the compilation error when it was encountered. For a task centered on generating working tests, non-compiling tests constitute complete failure of the primary objective. The transparent error reporting is appreciated but does not salvage a non-functional deliverable.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate tests with validation execution unavailable
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A delivered a comprehensive pytest suite with three test files covering all three requested modules and all requested behavior categories (validation, boundaries, rollover, truncation). It created detailed test implementations mapping 9+ specific behaviors to test artifacts, preserved production code unchanged, and honestly acknowledged that test execution was unavailable due to shell policy denial. Response B provided no tangible deliverables—it mentioned invoking a skill but produced no test files, no behavior coverage, and no implementation evidence. The rubric explicitly allows for execution denial without score reduction, but Response B fails on the more fundamental criterion of actually creating the requested tests. This is a clear case where one response completed the assigned work while the other did not.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve a classic MSTest project while adding broad coverage
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses successfully accomplish the core task of adding unit tests to the net472 MSTest fixture while preserving project format and dependencies. However, Response B demonstrates superior test design with finer-grained boundary condition separation (e.g., PercentageLessThanZero vs PercentageGreaterThanHundred rather than combined InvalidPercentage), more comprehensive TieredDiscountPolicy coverage (explicit rate boundary tests), and more rigorous evidence documentation with specific test method names. Response B also showed slightly more systematic investigation using ripgrep. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Audit a suite without editing it
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more structured, evidence-specific, and actionable while covering a somewhat broader set of important gaps. A is accurate and concise, and B's minor factual overstatement about an uncaught exception prevents a larger margin.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate a project-wide pytest suite across modules
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are transparent about the unrun test suite and provide credible pytest coverage. A is modestly stronger because its disclosed suite and evidence mapping are more comprehensive and explicitly cover additional requested boundary and truncation behaviors.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate collaborating Go package tests
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: skill, reverse: baseline). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate focused tests directly
judgeRationales.rationale: The actual implementation quality is effectively the same, including the inability to run tests. B is better because its final report is substantially more auditable: it names the tests and records exact assertions and validation failure details without overstating success.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate layered Vitest coverage for an async cart
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: skill, reverse: baseline). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate project-wide xUnit tests for a .NET library
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to have produced substantively appropriate suites and both honestly reported that execution was blocked. B is better chiefly because its final result is more auditable: it explicitly maps each requirement to named tests and more clearly records the unrun validation status. The gap is modest because A also appears to cover the required behavioral cases.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate tests with validation execution unavailable
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: skill, reverse: baseline). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve a classic MSTest project while adding broad coverage
judgeRationales.rationale: A delivers more complete behavioral coverage, especially the essential 0% and 100% DiscountService boundaries, and supplies stronger exact evidence. B is cleaner in avoiding A’s leftover temporary root project, but its apparent omission of those DiscountService boundaries is the more important quality gap.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Repair weak tests and close named gaps
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are successful and satisfy the core request, but B presents a more comprehensive, directly evidenced test suite, including an additional missing-item removal case and more granular assertions. The difference is meaningful but not large because A also added the requested coverage and passed the project tests.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Review focused assertions without a second audit agent
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the key distinction the task requires: several checks are hollow, but the item-count and computed-total checks do provide some behavioral protection. A's omission of the former and dismissal-by-omission of the latter makes its core assessment materially less accurate.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Assertion quality analysis
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more actionable and comprehensive, with a clearer per-test assessment and concrete recommendations for improving assertion quality. A is concise and accurate, and avoids B's apparent test-count inconsistency, but provides less useful detail overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Comprehensive test quality audit of weak test suite
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly conclude the suite provides false confidence and identify the principal anti-patterns and coverage gaps. B is stronger because it systematically accounts for every test, quantifies the weakness, and gives prioritized, concrete repairs. Its only notable flaw is imprecise wording that negative-price validation has no test, when the suite has an inadequate one. A is still solid but contains a factual error about an unhandled exception passing an assertion-free test and lacks actionable remediation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline request to generate new tests
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses fundamentally fail the supplied audit-oriented rubric because they generated tests and modified the project. A is marginally preferable because it did not alter the production ShoppingCart implementation, whereas B did.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose test smells and propose a repair order
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong and identify the central false-pass defects. B is better because it is more evidence-based, more precise about contract coverage and exception behavior, and explicitly avoids treating the valid state assertion as a smell.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identify behavior gaps that existing tests would miss
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more test-review-oriented: it supplies precise mutation examples, concrete assertions, and clearer risk-based prioritization. A is also strong and adds useful decimal-total coverage, but includes a more speculative price-change claim and is less explicit about regression mechanisms. Both miss empty-cart total coverage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Route a curated test list to per-test decisions
judgeRationales.rationale: B reaches both expected classifications and grades, notably the required B for ItemCount_AfterAdd, and includes a concrete fix for the failed test. A is more tightly formatted around the requested outcome/grade relationship, but its incorrect C grade is a substantive scoring error.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Targeted anti-pattern review
judgeRationales.rationale: Both reviews are accurate, concise, and identify the important test weaknesses. B is modestly stronger because it better categorizes the impact, ties gaps to the cart contract, and gives a clear prioritized remediation path.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Full pipeline: detect statics and recommend migration plan
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides the stronger technical migration direction through TimeProvider, System.IO.Abstractions, concrete call mappings, DI wiring, and identification of the double-clock-read correctness issue. A is admirably bounded and better at minimizing abstractions, but misses the key timestamp risk and does not recommend the requested modern built-in/library seams.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Inventory static dependencies without modifying the project
judgeRationales.rationale: A is more precise and focused on actual ambient dependencies, with clear categories, affected members, and actionable seams. B contributes the useful observation that CreateTrial's two clock reads may drift, but its unnecessary serialization concern and inconsistent call-site count reduce confidence slightly.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Leave an already injected clock unchanged
judgeRationales.rationale: The substantive conclusion and lack of changes are equally correct in both responses. B is marginally stronger because it reports a successful build validation, while A's build attempt was rejected.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate an instance clock with manual production construction
judgeRationales.rationale: The substantive implementations are effectively equivalent and satisfy the requested mechanical replacement. Response B is somewhat more explicit about constructor shape, while Response A is equally clear about the fallback behavior; neither has a demonstrated correctness advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate time dependencies and add deterministic tests
judgeRationales.rationale: The core TimeProvider injection and production registration are correct, and tests were run successfully. But the solution fails key task constraints: it alters CreateTrial's clock-read behavior, does not create the required sibling FullPipeline.Tests project, and inaccurately claims that it did. Multiple evaluator checks therefore fail.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Replace filesystem statics without touching unrelated dependencies
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: baseline). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Report a missing selected filesystem interface without inventing one
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: skill, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Targeted request: just migrate DateTime to TimeProvider
judgeRationales.rationale: The implementations appear equivalently correct and focused, but B provides stronger final-result assurance by reporting that the injected-clock behavioral contract passed. A was transparent that validation was blocked, but could not provide that confirmation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Avoid false positives when ambient resources are already abstracted
judgeRationales.rationale: Both outputs correctly conclude that there are zero remaining seams, identify all relevant existing injections, and appropriately exempt deterministic path manipulation. B is marginally more specific with line references, while A is marginally terser; neither has a meaningful quality advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect statics inside lambda expressions and LINQ queries
judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantially more actionable and verifiable through per-call-site line references and method-level impact analysis. Its erroneous inclusion of the FileInfo instance member as a static dependency and resulting inflated total prevent a larger margin; A is broadly correct but less complete at the call-site level.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect time-related statics and recommend TimeProvider
judgeRationales.rationale: The findings are effectively identical and correct. A is marginally stronger overall because its example and production/test guidance make the recommended refactor more directly actionable; B's handling of local time is a small countervailing strength.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Exclude obj and bin directories from the scan
judgeRationales.rationale: Both successfully exclude build artifacts and find the important production static calls, but B is more complete and decision-useful as a report while avoiding A's unnecessary false-positive-style recommendations for Main and Path.Combine. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identify static dependencies in a multi-class project
judgeRationales.rationale: Both outputs are accurate and useful, but B is a substantially more complete scan report: it enumerates counts and locations, includes omitted hard-to-test dependencies such as Guid and serialization, explicitly catches inline HttpClient construction, and provides a prioritized remediation plan. A remains a correct concise summary.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Keep one authoritative total with file line locations and no seam for pure helpers
judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantially closer to an actionable, correctly scoped audit: it has a complete location ledger, correctly excludes pure Path.Combine, and captures Guid.NewGuid and HttpClient construction. Its important defect is omitting ambient-state Path.GetTempPath, so its total should be 28 rather than 27. A internally reconciles but wrongly counts and recommends pure path operations while omitting Guid and HttpClient construction, producing a materially less reliable audit. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for Python timezone review
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are concise, correct, file-grounded answers that avoid modifying files. B is marginally more technically precise about Django timezone configuration.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Verify structured report includes file count, categories, and top patterns
judgeRationales.rationale: B fulfills every requested reporting element with complete, reconciled totals and detailed evidence. A gets the file count and several major patterns right but materially misses static/testability dependencies and consequently understates categories and worst-offender counts.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Analyse a CI Cobertura report without re-running tests or installing tools
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers correctly use the supplied Cobertura report without rerunning tests and identify the same primary risk. B is stronger because it quantitatively supports the hotspot ranking with complexity and CRAP, while remaining concise.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Coverage plateau diagnosis
judgeRationales.rationale: A accurately identifies the main blocker and supplies useful, specific GPA test cases without inventing a coverage projection. B usefully reports Enroll's 15/16 status, but its central quantitative claim (81% after fully covering CalculateGpa) is seriously wrong and it incorrectly calls CalculateGpa the entire gap. Both omit an explicit Enroll test recommendation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Distinguish partially covered branches from covered lines
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers are substantively correct and satisfy the core explanation. B is preferable because it avoids presenting unsupported hypothetical Enroll predicates as a detailed test inventory while still covering the relevant compound-condition caveat. A is more detailed, but that detail introduces the principal rubric violation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve a classic packages.config project when coverage data is absent
judgeRationales.rationale: Both fail the central requirement to avoid coverage/CRAP conclusions without Cobertura data. A is marginally more appropriately cautious and flags the lack of meaningful behavior, while B converts a passing trivial test into unsupported exact coverage and CRAP claims.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Project-wide coverage analysis with existing Cobertura data
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are accurate, concise coverage analyses grounded in the supplied XML. B has a particularly readable method table and target arithmetic, but A more thoroughly connects uncovered coverage evidence to exact source behaviors and test cases, making it marginally more useful.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Reconcile a coverage target spread across several members
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are arithmetically correct and satisfy the core request. B is more complete in its risk-based priority justification and identifies the minimal sufficient test scope. Its awkward sentence about 'both top single hotspots' does not undermine its otherwise clear, correct conclusion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Refactoring safety assessment from coverage data
judgeRationales.rationale: A provides a clearer, more actionable risk stratification—safe, guarded, and blind—and appropriately treats partially covered Enroll differently from the much riskier methods. Both miss the rubric's requested CRAP/complexity-based analysis, so the advantage is limited.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Run coverage from scratch without existing data
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide accurate baseline coverage and sensible hotspot guidance. B is stronger overall because it fulfills the risk-analysis dimension with evidence-based complexity and CRAP scoring/ranking, while A is stronger only in explicitly naming coverlet and giving a more detailed test list.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for behavioral gap analysis
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers are concise, evidence-based, and comply with the request not to modify files. B is modestly stronger because it clearly explains why merely executing a guard is insufficient and gives more cautious, relevant examples of the evidence needed.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for one-member CRAP analysis
judgeRationales.rationale: The responses are substantively equivalent: both are properly scoped and concise, but both make the same material CRAP-formula error and therefore report the wrong score and an assessment based on it.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for static source-to-test pairing
judgeRationales.rationale: A gives the appropriate, honest limitation and asks for the missing repository input. B's confident empty-result conclusion is unsupported and fails the central task setup.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for test trait distribution
judgeRationales.rationale: A actually audited and modified an existing NUnit test fixture, counted category applications transparently, and built it successfully. B manufactured a new test project and suite instead of auditing the existing tests, making its classifications and counts nonresponsive despite a passing test run. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.rationale: The substantive code change and validation appear equivalent and correct in both runs. B's final report is slightly stronger because it clearly documents the exact scoped production and test files changed, matching the requested migration-summary scope.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline migration when wrapper does not exist yet
judgeRationales.rationale: B produces a compiling migration using the conventional System.IO.Abstractions IFileSystem and correctly adds its package, making its implementation more technically aligned than A's custom wrapper that retains File.ReadAllText. However, both substantially fail the key authorization/stop requirement, and B's claim that no File.ReadAllText usages remained is misleading because its verification found the intended instance call.

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate a static helper class without breaking its callers
judgeRationales.rationale: The available evidence indicates both runs delivered the same required static, AsyncLocal-scoped TimeProvider design and passing focused tests. B's summary is slightly more implementation-specific, but that does not establish a material difference in the resulting code quality.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate environment access to an existing reader and update tests
judgeRationales.rationale: A is preferable because it meets the injection goal while retaining the SystemEnvironmentReader-backed default production path. Both otherwise appear similarly scoped and validated, and neither provides clear evidence of explicit null/missing-value test coverage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate file calls to an existing custom store and remove real I/O tests
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Migrate only in scoped files, leaving others untouched
judgeRationales.rationale: The implementations appear equivalently correct, scoped, and build-validated. B has a modestly better final report through exact file paths and explicit accounting of all four migrated reads and the preserved out-of-scope call.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve DateTimeKind when migrating to TimeProvider
judgeRationales.rationale: The substantive CouponService migration appears correct in both responses, but B is more faithful to the requested minimal pure refactor by not making unrelated DI-registration changes.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve DateTimeOffset values during TimeProvider migration
judgeRationales.rationale: The resulting code and scope are effectively identical and correct in both runs. B is slightly better because it explicitly communicates the successful build validation in its final answer.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve local calendar semantics when migrating DateTime.Now
judgeRationales.rationale: Both runs largely complete the scoped migration and validate it with a successful build, but B uses the precise LocalDateTime.Date expression required to preserve the original local DateTime semantics. A's shorter GetLocalNow().Date variant is close but does not meet that specified implementation/Kind-preservation detail.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Audit a suite without editing it
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more structured and actionable, with concrete correction examples and a clear remediation order. A is marginally more complete on coverage nuances, but B better communicates the audit's practical outcome. B's characterization of the sleep issue as high severity is somewhat overstated, so the advantage is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate a project-wide pytest suite across modules
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides a more coherent, comprehensive coverage map and stronger explicit boundary rationale. The advantage is limited because neither response could run pytest, and both were appropriately transparent about that limitation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate collaborating Go package tests
judgeRationales.rationale: The substantive test work is broadly comparable, but B presents stronger, auditable evidence of requirement coverage and more clearly communicates the unverified validation status. Neither demonstrated that go test ./... actually passes.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate focused tests directly
judgeRationales.rationale: The substantive implementation appears comparable, and both failed to run the required tests because shell execution was blocked. B nevertheless gives a clearer account of the concrete expected behavior and manual verification, making its final report more useful and auditable.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate layered Vitest coverage for an async cart
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to implement a broadly appropriate fake-based Vitest suite but leave execution and coverage unverified. B is stronger in transparent reporting and requirement-to-test evidence, while A has a minor internal inconsistency and less structured validation disclosure.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate project-wide xUnit tests for a .NET library
judgeRationales.rationale: The substantive suites appear similarly comprehensive, but B is better evidenced: it names the individual tests, demonstrates requirement mapping, and verifies a fresh build/test run with all 19 tests passing. A's transparent inability to run is not misleading, but leaves its result unverified.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Generate tests with validation execution unavailable
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are honest about the execution limitation and appear to have created comprehensive suites. B is stronger in its final reporting: it clearly marks the result partial, avoids overclaiming coverage, and gives an actionable, named mapping from requirements to test artifacts.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve a classic MSTest project while adding broad coverage
judgeRationales.rationale: The underlying implementation appears substantially equivalent and appropriately scoped in both runs. B’s final report is more directly auditable, mapping each requested behavior to a specific test and clearly separating static evidence from unrun execution. A has a small stated coverage advantage for the zero-rate policy boundary, so the overall advantage is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Repair weak tests and close named gaps
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: skill, reverse: baseline). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Review focused assertions without a second audit agent
judgeRationales.rationale: A is substantively more coherent and correctly classifies the two meaningful assertions. B contains a major internal inconsistency by saying no tests provide behavioral protection while later explicitly calling two assertions meaningful. Both could be more tightly scoped by omitting broader coverage-gap recommendations.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +66.7% (4W/2T/0L over 6 preference-eligible stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.063), mean preference +28.6% across 7 paired run(s), 1 dormancy stimulus/stimuli excluded from preference — not credible — 2 of 6 preference-eligible stimulus vote(s) tied, leaving only 4 discordant preference vote(s). The sign test conditions on non-tie stimulus votes and cannot reach 0.05 below 5, so no record could have passed here — this is not a measured null. Either the agent is inert on these scenarios (make them discriminate) or the eval needs more distinct stimuli to clear the ties — native evaluator reported an objective task-completion regression

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: baseline, reverse: skill). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Comprehensive test quality audit of weak test suite
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more systematic, accounts for the suite test-by-test, distinguishes sound versus weak checks, and offers concrete prioritized repairs. Its main weaknesses are a few exaggerated claims about tests being unable to fail under any implementation and a brief self-correction in the ledger. A is accurate and concise, but its unexplained seven-versus-six test count and less actionable prioritization make it weaker overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline request to generate new tests
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses fundamentally failed the audit-oriented rubric because they generated and modified tests rather than redirecting without changes. B is marginally preferable because it made fewer unrelated project changes and did not claim successful verification after altering project configuration.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose test smells and propose a repair order
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are accurate and actionable, but B is more disciplined in separating ineffective tests from valid focused assertions. That precision better supports maintainable test repair while preserving existing useful coverage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identify behavior gaps that existing tests would miss
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: skill, reverse: baseline). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Route a curated test list to per-test decisions
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are correct and PR-usable on the core verdicts. B is stronger because it provides concrete fixes and explicit per-test mutation rationale, though it is less compact than requested and includes some unnecessary extra detail.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Targeted anti-pattern review
judgeRationales.rationale: Both reviews are accurate and cover the important weaknesses. B is more useful because it includes precise, test-specific fixes, severity grouping, and a positive note about the valid test. Its duplicated fifth critical finding and somewhat inflated severity count keep the advantage modest rather than large.
